PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review

Hua Yang1, Aditya Bhardwaj1, Shidong Pan2 and Bowen Xu1 Affiliation: 1North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA
{hyang45, arbhardw, bxu22}@ncsu.edu Affiliation: 2Independent Researcher
Shidong.Pan@anu.edu.au
Abstract

Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM’s GDPR-principle assignments.

Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42–51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88–91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11–15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.

Index Terms: 
privacy, GDPR, code review, pull requests, coding agents, dataset

I Introduction

Privacy laws such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [1] and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) [2] require software to protect the personal data it processes. Yet developers often find these requirements vague, costly, and difficult to operationalize [3, 4, 5, 6], and privacy violations often surface only after release, through audits of deployed applications [7] or reports in app reviews [8] and issue trackers [9]. Code review is therefore a critical opportunity to catch privacy defects before they are merged and shipped. At the same time, code review is increasingly moving to coding agents. Agents already resolve real GitHub issues (e.g., [10, 11]) and are deployed as reviewers: at Atlassian, 38.7% of an LLM reviewer’s comments led to code changes [12]. However, review agents solve only about 40% of c-CRAB’s tasks [13], while existing automated-review benchmarks focus primarily on functional defects [14], leaving non-functional requirements such as privacy comparatively unexplored. As coding agents increasingly both produce and review code, an important question is whether they can identify privacy defects before those defects are merged. Evaluating this capability requires real code changes in which a privacy defect can be linked to the fix developers accepted and the surrounding review context. Such data are largely absent.

In this paper, we introduce PrivacyPR, which closes three gaps in existing data. (1) Traceability. Privacy-law mining studies classify issues and commits by topic or change type, but do not link a concrete privacy defect to its accepted fix and review [9, 15, 16]. PrivacyPR provides this traceability by pairing each privacy defect, such as personal data written to logs or a missing consent check, with the merged fix and its review discussion (Fig. 1). (2) Coverage. Existing privacy benchmarks are limited in scope; for example, GDPR-Bench-Android covers violations from only 15 Android repositories [17]. PrivacyPR contains 1,169 privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs from 1,048 repositories across platforms, to our knowledge the largest cross-project dataset of labeled privacy fixes, with each fix further labeled by fix type and GDPR Art. 5(1) principles. (3) Evaluation. Existing code review benchmarks target functional defects [14, 13] or security [18], not privacy. PrivacyPR therefore provides Verified, a manually checked test split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, together with an evaluation harness that turns real fixes into review tasks for systematically comparing reviewers, prompts, and coding agents (Section III).

II Dataset Construction

II-A Search and Filtering (Steps A1–A2)

Fig. 2A shows the construction pipeline. Step A1 queries GitHub’s search API for merged, non-draft PRs whose title or body contains one of 17 keywords (matched by word stem). Eleven come from privacy-law mining studies [3, 15, 16, 9] (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, anonymization, cookie banner, privacy violation) and six recurred in privacy PRs seen during collection (e.g., user consent, PII leak, Right to Erasure). A pilot of about ten LLM-labeled PRs per term dropped seven terms with at most 36% privacy PRs. As the API returns at most 1,000 results per query, we query each keyword one year at a time and stop at 2,000 PRs so that frequent keywords do not dominate. Four keywords hit this cap, and three of them stop early: GDPR after 2019, cookie banner after 2021 and user consent after 2022. Deduplicating by URL gives 11,964 PRs. Step A2 keeps repositories with at least 100 stars (as of March 2026), a proxy for active projects, leaving 4,133 PRs from 1,469 repositories. Keyword search is noisy (63% false positives in [9]), so annotation (Step A4) separates privacy fixes from other PRs.

II-B Enrichment and Storage (Step A3)

In Step A3, one GraphQL query per PR retrieves its metadata (title, body, author, timestamps, branches) and up to 100 each of its commits, changed files, closing issues, comments, reviews and review threads (50 comments per thread); the diff of every changed file comes from the paginated REST endpoint /pulls/{number}/files. Two PRs that no longer resolve are dropped, leaving 4,131 records from the same 1,469 repositories. Each record is one JSON object with all of the above, the patches (digests in the release, Step A5) and the LLM annotation with the raw response.

II-C Annotation (Step A4)

LLM annotation. In Step A4, every PR is annotated by Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (gemini-2.5-flash-lite), chosen for its low cost. The prompt renders the PR as text (title, description, commits, changed files, closing issues, comments, reviews and threads, and diffs truncated to 3,000 characters per file, which affects 21.3% of patches) and defines the JSON output of Table I with one worked example and criteria for is_privacy_related (the PR addresses the handling or protection of personal data or mitigates risks such as data leakage). The auxiliary fields rest on commit messages, as the model sees no per-commit diffs. A second parser recovers 132 of 139 unparseable raw responses; seven PRs have no usable label.

Manual validation (Fig. 2, B2). Two recruited annotators, each holding at least a master’s degree and two years of software engineering experience, complete a training session on the GDPR principles and the annotation schema. They then independently check the 650 LLM-screened candidates of the test split (Section III), seeing the model’s labels. Each judges is_privacy_related of every candidate as correct, partially correct or incorrect from the PR page and diff, and the other fields of the 300 fixes, except buggy_commit and confidence, as endorsed or not. Because they see the labels, the endorsement rates in Table III may be inflated. One annotator later checks 50 random Small defect descriptions.

II-D Scrubbing and Release (Steps A5–A6)

Step A5 removes author logins and names and replaces e-mail addresses and the names written next to them; @mentions, branch names and PR URLs remain. Patches, as third-party code, become SHA-256 digests that a script rehydrates and verifies. Step A6 releases PrivacyPR at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765 as JSON Lines in three splits: Full, the 1,169 PRs labeled privacy fixes with confidence 5, the 1,643 non-fix PRs and the seven unlabeled ones (2,819 PRs from 1,048 repositories); and Verified and Small, 250 + 250 and 100 + 100 PRs whose privacy label both annotators accepted (Section III). The 1,312 fixes with confidence 2–4 are released separately, together with the collection code, the harness, the Small reviews and judge verdicts, and the annotators’ verdicts. Data are under CC BY 4.0, code under MIT.

II-E Statistics and Label Quality

Distribution (Table II). Of the 4,124 PRs with a usable label, 2,481 are labeled privacy-related, 1,169 with confidence 5. Non-fix PRs mostly get confidence 1 (89.8%), so the field reads as privacy relevance; the fixes span the whole window (148–265 per year). Half of the fixes (49.2%) combine several types. Only 260 fixes (22.2%) cite a GDPR article, 91 of them exactly Art. 5 and 32, as in the prompt’s example, so these counts and the integrity share may echo it.

Typical fixes. Integrity and confidentiality, the most frequent principle, mostly concerns personal data leaking through logs, debug output or APIs: kubernetes #108631 drops a user-identifying field from the HTTP log, and smart-answers #5720 filters vaccination status from the application log. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency fixes add or repair consent flows and notices: wp-calypso #34187 shows the GDPR banner at signup, and the PR in Fig. 1 blocks e-mails sent without consent. Data minimisation fixes stop collecting or transmitting identifiers that are not needed: fastlane #12869 enables IP anonymization in analytics, and kubermatic #3854 drops user name and e-mail from its metrics.

Code changes and review. Privacy fixes are larger, more discussed and slower to merge than non-fix PRs (Table II), most of all access control, data removal and encryption fixes. The LLM labels 52 fixes (4.4%) as raised by a reviewer and fixed in a later commit, an upper bound (see below).

Label quality (Table III). A and B are the two human annotators of Section II-C. On the privacy label they agree on 82–89% of the PRs but κ\kappa is low: most verdicts are correct, which raises chance agreement, and they questioned mostly different, borderline PRs. On the finer fields, both endorse 72% of the principle labels and 52% of the fix types in Verified; the rest are mostly labels that A endorses and B questions (both reject only 4 and 19 of 300), which keeps κ\kappa near chance. Users should restrict to labels both endorsed, or inspect the contested ones, with the released verdicts. fixed_commit often points at a clean-up or merge commit, and few during review labels are endorsed, so the 52 review-raised fixes are an upper bound.

Precision of Full. A and B judge 299 and 298 of the 300 confidence-5 test fixes at least partly privacy fixes; as GPT-6.1 screened them and larger PRs are not covered, the precision of Full is likely lower.

III Use Case: Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review

Verified and Small. The harness (Fig. 2B) draws, in a seeded order (B1), privacy fixes with confidence 5 and, as controls, non-fix PRs labeled not privacy-related, by descending confidence; each class has at most five PRs per repository and 1–10 changed files, at least one of them code. GPT-6.1 describes each candidate fix’s defect from its label and diff, or reports none, and checks from the diff alone that each non-fix PR fixes no privacy defect; inconsistent candidates are discarded. The first 250 remaining candidates per class whose label both annotators judged correct (B2) form Verified; the first 100 per class form Small. Selection favors small, clean PRs (673 of 1,169 confidence-5 fixes qualify) and easy controls.

Reviewers (B3). Three single calls, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.7 Flash and 3.8 Flash, span three cost tiers and see only the changed files and the diff. Two open-source coding agents, Gemini CLI 0.64.0 and SWE-agent 1.1.0, run on 3.7 Flash, so that comparing them with a single 3.7 Flash call isolates what the agent adds; they review inside the full repository (Docker, 60-minute limit, no web access; all runs October 2026).

Test design (B3–B5). Each PR of Small is a task that checks out the repository at its head and presents the reversed diff, without documentation and changelogs, as the change to review, so for a fix it reintroduces the defect. Each fix is also reviewed forward, to see whether its known defect is claimed, and the non-fix PRs measure false alarms. Each reviewer gets a generic and a privacy review prompt. Two judges, GPT-6.1 (gpt-6.1-sol) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (preview), decide whether a review identifies the described defect, raises a privacy issue on a non-fix PR or claims that defect in the original fix (Cohen’s κ\kappa between them 0.70–0.97); we report GPT-6.1’s verdicts (Gemini 3.1 Pro’s detection rates differ by at most 4 points).

Results (Fig. 3). Asking about privacy raises detection for every reviewer (exact McNemar test, p<0.001p<0.001); 95% bootstrap intervals over repositories span about ±\pm10 points. On the same model, the agents identify 88–91% of the defects, 77–82% as high severity, against 59% and 29% for a single call, but also raise privacy issues on 11–15% of the non-fix PRs, against 1%. Some may be real, as these PRs match privacy keywords. With the privacy prompt, the agents also claim the known defect in 13–21% of the original fixes (single calls: 4–10%), so they are more sensitive but less specific. Agents also cost more: 3.6–5.2 minutes and $0.14–0.18 per review vs 14 s and $0.013 for one call.

Takeaways. First, the prompt matters more than the model tier: the cheapest single call with the privacy prompt (64%) beats the best single call (23%) and both agents (42–51%) under the generic prompt. Second, repository access is what the agents add: on the same model, detection rises from 59% to 88–91%, but at about ten times the cost and ten times the false alarms. Third, the agents claim a defect in 13–21% of the correct fixes, about as often as they flag non-fix PRs, which suggests that they react to code that touches personal data rather than reason about the defect. Unless asked, every tested reviewer misses about half or more of these defects.

IV Discussion

Uses and implications. Researchers can study how privacy defects arise, are discussed and are fixed, and which fix types and principles recur. Tool builders can test classifiers of privacy-relevant changes on Verified, train them on the rest of Full, and compare reviewers, prompts and models on Small. Practitioners who adopt agent-based review should ask for privacy explicitly (Section III); the fix types offer a checklist for such prompts, and the principle labels link each fix to a GDPR obligation.

Limitations. PrivacyPR relies on keyword retrieval and a single LLM annotation run, so it may miss privacy fixes and retain label noise; human validation covered only relatively small PRs and annotators saw the model labels. The schema maps CCPA and cookie-rule fixes to GDPR principles and omits some concepts, such as accountability and data-subject rights. The evaluation also has construct-validity risks: GPT-6.1 generates defect descriptions, screens tasks, and judges reviews; reverting fixes may expose easier cues than naturally occurring defects; each agent setting was run once; and all evaluated reviewers use Gemini models that may have seen the public fixes during training.

Ethics. We process public GitHub data for research as a legitimate interest (GDPR Art. 6(1)(f)), with the scrubbing of Step A5 as an Art. 89(1) safeguard; this paper and the README inform developers (Art. 14(5)(b)), who can ask hyang45@ncsu.edu to be removed. PR text went to the Vertex AI and OpenAI APIs, which do not train on API data.

V Related Work

Prior work mines privacy law in repositories: Hennig et al. coded 652 issues on data protection [9], Franke et al. compared 15,731 “GDPR” PRs with others by activity metrics [3], and Kapitsaki et al. coded 594 commits and 1,186 issues mentioning privacy laws by relevance, topic and whether they change code or text [15, 16]; these works label samples by hand or not at all. For compliance detection, GDPR-Bench-Android has 1,951 manually annotated violations in 15 Android repositories [17], LLMs [19] and policy checks [20] target apps, and static analysis points reviewers to code that processes personal data [21]. Among code review benchmarks, SWR-Bench [14] and c-CRAB [13] evaluate review on PRs or diffs, and SeRe [18] and SecureReviewer [22] target security, as do the vulnerability-fix datasets CVEfixes [23] and MoreFixes [24]; none labels privacy compliance. Unlike these works, PrivacyPR pairs defects with accepted fixes and review, labels every PR, and ships a verified test split with a harness.

VI Conclusion

This paper presents PrivacyPR, a cross-project dataset of 1,169 privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs from 1,048 GitHub repositories, with LLM-generated privacy labels and human-validated test splits. Our evaluation shows that current reviewers, including coding agents, detect substantially more privacy defects when explicitly prompted to review for privacy. We release all artifacts for reproducible research.
